analysis.one_liner: Bans new municipal trash incinerators until 2000 and imposes strict health, recycling, and local-veto conditions on hazardous waste incinerators.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 86 cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have blocked permits for new or expanded municipal trash incinerators until 2000, and after that allowed them only if communities first hit high recycling targets, the facility provably would not harm health or property values, and the local government approved it. It would have treated incinerator ash as hazardous waste requiring sealed landfills, banned burning batteries, chlorinated plastics, electronics, and household hazardous waste, and imposed similar health, disclosure, and community-veto conditions on hazardous waste incinerators. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near existing or proposed incinerators — often neighborhoods in industrial areas — who face air emissions, contaminated ash, and falling property values. Communities that gain the right to approve or block a facility in their own boundaries, with a $50,000 technical assistance grant to hire their own experts. Recycling and composting operations, which the bill would drive material toward instead of burners.

how_it_helps.text: It places a moratorium on permits for new or expanded municipal solid waste incinerators until the year 2000, halting construction of facilities that emit pollutants and generate toxic ash [S2][S3].

After 2000, no incinerator could be permitted unless the applicant proves high diversion rates (80% of metals, 65% of glass and paper, 50% of plastics), proves the facility will not harm health, property values, or the local economy, proves it is cheaper than recycling, and wins approval from the local government where it would sit [S2][S3].

Local community groups would receive a $50,000 technical assistance grant — renewed every six months — so residents could afford their own experts during the permitting fight, and every facility would require a full environmental impact statement [S2][S3].

Incinerator ash would be treated as hazardous waste and must go into specially engineered, double-lined ash-only landfills, ending uses of ash in products or fill where its toxins could contact people [S2][S3].
Burning household hazardous waste, batteries, chlorinated plastics (a source of dioxins), consumer electronics, and yard waste in municipal incinerators would be banned [S2][S3].

Hazardous waste incinerator permits would require waste composition analyses, proof that no safer disposal technology exists, corporate disclosure of criminal and environmental convictions, community grants, local approval, and proof that states and generators are cutting toxic chemical use by 50% within five years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Waste-to-energy incineration companies and hazardous waste disposal firms, which would face a moratorium, strict new permit tests, and hazardous-waste-grade ash handling. Municipalities and utilities that had signed long-term contracts counting on burning trash for power, which would bear retrofit or closure costs. Taxpayers and ratepayers could face higher disposal costs in places where recycling infrastructure is not yet built out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incinerator operators and municipalities relying on them

drawbacks.text: An eight-year moratorium leaves communities without an approved path for waste disposal if recycling and composting capacity lags; waste that cannot be diverted may end up in ordinary landfills, which carry their own environmental risks [S2][S3].
Existing incinerators would have three years to move their ash into expensive double-lined monofills, a cost that would fall on the municipalities and ratepayers those facilities serve [S3].

The permit tests are so demanding — including proving a facility will not negatively affect property values and is cheaper than recycling over its whole life — that opponents argued they amount to a near-permanent ban rather than a standard, potentially stalling facilities that some growing regions saw as needed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and community-control benefits are substantial: dioxin and heavy-metal emissions drop when batteries and chlorinated plastics are kept out of burners, ash stops being used casually, and residents get funded experts plus a local veto. The honest cost is transition risk — if recycling lags, waste shifts to landfills, and existing incinerator towns face higher ash-disposal bills. The bill's design bets heavily on forcing recycling to scale up before any new burning is allowed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its hazardous materials subcommittee for a year and a half and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Kostmayer introduced the bill on August 2, 1991, with 15 original cosponsors [S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 27, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, where it remained [S5].
Support grew to 86 cosponsors — 79 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S4].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, and the bill died in subcommittee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incineration and hazardous waste disposal companies, and the municipalities with sunk investments in burning trash, are better off because the bill never moved; communities near proposed facilities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incinerator operators and waste disposal firms

for.name: Rep. Peter H. Kostmayer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; added 45 more sponsors in January 1992.

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 79 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 79 of 86 cosponsors were Democrats, though 6 Republicans and 1 Independent signed on — and the bill died in a committee led by a Democrat without a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill freezes new construction until 2000 and sets nearly insurmountable permit conditions afterward, cutting off a revenue stream built on long-term municipal contracts. Its emissions and ash fall hardest on nearby residents.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste disposal and treatment firms (including cement kilns burning hazardous waste)
industries.note: New permits would require proof that no safer technology exists, corporate disclosure of criminal and environmental convictions, and toxics-use-reduction programs — conditions that would block many facilities. The bill explicitly covers cement kilns and industrial furnaces that burn hazardous waste.

industries.industry: Municipalities and public utilities with incinerator investments
industries.note: Governments that financed incinerators would bear the cost of moving ash into double-lined monofills within three years and lose the option to expand. The bill pushes their waste streams toward cheaper recycling and composting over the long run.

No new incinerator could be permitted until communities divert 65-90% of glass, paper, metals, yard waste, and plastics, and the EPA can raise those targets — directly feeding volume to recyclers and composters.
